tei:bibl.tei:title: תְּחִנַּת שָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיכֶם
Shalom Aleikhem teḥinah after lighting the Shabbat candles (1600)
tei:bibl.tei:note: Source: Teḥinah for Shalom Aleikhem from Birkhat ha-Mazon (Basel, 1600) https://opensiddur.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/tehinah-for-shalom-aleikhem-from-birkhat-ha-mazon-basel-1600.png
Converted from the export of opensiddur.org at 624215eef0.

tei:div.tei:p: From Dr. Morris Faierstein’s 2022 article, “An Early Modern Version of Shalom Aleichem for Women after Friday Candle Lighting” in Women in Judaism, 19(2), pp. 3–4:

The Hebrew text of this version of Shalom Aleikhem for women is found on the last page in the Basel edition of the [collection of prayers entitled] Birkhat ha-Mazon (Basel: Waldkirch, 1600). Perhaps its placement indicates an expectation that it will be recited regularly. It begins like Shalom Aleikhem and then continues in a form that resembles the latter part of the Ribon Olamim (Sovereign of the Universe) hymn. In other words, it is in classic teḥinah form, asking for the blessings normative for Teḥinot. This teḥinah is unusual in that it is in Hebrew and not in Yiddish as is normative for Teḥinot for women. The answer is found in the same Talmudic passage that prohibits petitioning for healing on the Sabbath. The rabbis state (in B. Shabbat 12b) there that the angels only understand Hebrew, and this teḥinah specifically addresses the angels. Thus, in order to be effective, the Teḥinah must be in Hebrew, so that the angels will understand what is being asked of them. In any event, the key Hebrew terms are part of the Hebrew component of Yiddish, so that anyone conversant in Yiddish would have a general idea of what is being asked in this Teḥinah....

Moshe Henochs Altschul-Yerushalmi, the author of the influential Yiddish ethical text, Sefer Brantshpigl (Cracow, 1596), writes about a woman who lights the Sabbath and Festival candles: “The sages write, when someone lights with good intentions then one fulfills the commandment to honor God, blessed be He, and to honor the Sabbath and the festivals, it is accorded for her as if she lit the candelabrum in the Temple.”

This is the Hebrew text of a teḥinah for Shalom Aleikhem intended for women lighting candles on the commencement of Shabbat and festival days as found on the last page in the Basel edition of the [collection of prayers entitled] Birkhat ha-Mazon (Basel: Waldkirch, 1600). The English translation is by Rabbi Dr. Morris M. Faierstein as published in “An Early Modern Version of Shalom Aleichem for Women after Friday Candle Lighting” in Women in Judaism, 19:2 (2022), on page 4. The text of the prayer itself was transcribed from the digital facsimile of the page image with the prayer appended to Dr. Faierstein’s article. I have parsed the text of the prayer by phrase and set it in a linear format side-by-side with Dr. Faierstein’s translation. Any thematic changes or changes of address (to the angels or Hashem) are indicated with paragraph breaks for clarity and ease-of-use by practitioners. In parsing the prayer, I have made some very light (or subtle changes in the punctuation indicating the change in where the prayer is address to the angels and where the prayer is addressed to Hashem. Many thanks to Nili Simḥai for bringing this prayer and Dr. Faierstein’s work on it to our attention. –Aharon Varady

tei:note.tei:p: For the origins and early history of tehinot see, Morris M. Faierstein, “The Earliest Published Yiddish Tehinnot (1590–1609).” Hebrew Union College Annual 91 (2020): 157–206.
Sefer Brantshpigl (Basel, 1602), 134a. His comment is an allusion to Zohar, I:48b.
